table.brief: Two sibling sub-columns under "Price" where one holds short numbers ($12) and the other long qualifiers ("$12 per seat per month, billed annually")

understanding.purpose: Compare six business software subscription plans on headline price, billing terms, minimum seats, contract, and support so a buyer can choose a plan.
understanding.reading: Readers scan down the Plan column and across the short comparison columns; they use List price as the quick numeric anchor, read Billing terms as explanatory prose, and compare Minimum seats, Contract, and Support as procurement constraints.
groups: Plan is the row identifier and reading anchor.
List price and Billing terms form the Price group, but List price is a short numeric key while Billing terms is explanatory prose.
Minimum seats, Contract, and Support are short constraint/comparison columns that should be scanned together across rows.
keep_intact: Plan names such as Enterprise, and the Plan header
List prices such as $12 and numeric minimum-seat values
Contract terms and support-level labels, including their longest words
Headers should not break mid-word; Billing terms especially needs its full label width
may_wrap: The List price and Minimum seats headers at spaces
Longer Contract and Support phrases at spaces, never inside words

preferred.name: r2A
preferred.note: Move 10px from Billing terms to Contract while keeping Support at r1A's 134px. Contract 100px should fit 'Annual only' on one line; Billing 214px preserves r1A's 2/3-line prose pattern, though '12-month' may break at its hyphen.

acceptable.name: r2B
acceptable.note: Keep r1B's safe 102px Contract, take 5px from Billing and give 5px to Support. Support 130px should pull the Team and Education labels back to two lines; Billing 216px remains close to r1A's prose width.

acceptable.name: r2C
acceptable.note: Prioritize the right-hand comparison columns: Contract 102px and Support 136px, with Billing reduced to 210px. This tests whether easier scanning of Contract and Support is worth the tighter Billing prose, which may gain a line in the longest cells.

acceptable.name: r3B
acceptable.note: Tests the other way to fund the prose column: keep Contract at 102 (81 content) so 'Annual only' stays on one line, and take the width from Support instead — 136→126 (105 content) — so Billing terms gets 220 (199 content), its widest, with the cleanest breaks. Support accepts a 3-line 'Dedicated / success / manager' only in the Enterprise row, which is already 3 lines tall because of Billing terms, so no row grows.

acceptable.name: r1A
acceptable.note: From r0B, reclaim 43px from Minimum seats (130→87; the header wraps inside the merged two-row header), add 34px to Support (100→134), 6px to Contract (84→90), and 3px to Billing (221→224). This keeps List price one-line, keeps Billing safely in the 3-line range, makes Contract consistently 2 lines without mid-word splits, and gives Support enough width for most labels to be 2 lines. Sum 719.

acceptable.name: r3C
acceptable.note: Pushes the height-setting column to its practical maximum: Billing 226 (205 content) for the most relaxed prose wrapping, funded by Contract at 89 (68 content, uniform two lines) and Support at 133 (112 content, three lines on 'Dedicated success manager' only). Keeps Plan/Minimum seats at their hard floors and holds Support at or below the prose column's line count so nothing new becomes the tallest cell.

bad.name: r1B
bad.note: Alternative from r0B: take 43px from Minimum seats, add 18px to Contract (84→102) and 25px to Support (100→125), leaving Billing at 221 and List at 88. This keeps “Annual only” close to one line and “Monthly or annual” at two lines, while preserving r0B’s safe Billing measure. Support 125 handles short phrases well but longer support labels may take 3 lines. Choose this if single-line Contract labels matter more than maximum Support measure. Sum 719.
bad.why: The Support column is squeezed to 125px, forcing repeated three-line support cells and a 547px table; the extra height does not buy a better Billing or Contract column.

bad.name: r3A
bad.note: Refines r2C: Contract 102→89 (content 68) so every Contract cell is a uniform two lines ('Monthly or' / 'annual', 'Annual' / 'only') instead of a 1-line/2-line mix, and that 13px goes to Billing terms (210→216, 195 content), restoring comfortable prose breaks. Support 143 (122 content) keeps 'Dedicated success' and 'Community forum' on one line with real margin instead of r2C's 1px margin. Plan 96 and Minimum seats 87 remain at their word floors.
bad.why: Contract at 89px fragments short categorical values into 'Annual / only' and 'Monthly / or annual' while the table is still 524px tall, so the poor break does not even buy compactness.

rationale: Billing terms is the only prose column and should receive the largest share; r2A gives it 214px while keeping Contract at 100px so 'Annual only' stays intact and 'Monthly or annual' breaks at a natural phrase boundary. Support can wrap, but at 134px most short support phrases stay to two lines, which keeps the table from ballooning. The 500px designs gain height by starving Contract, fragmenting a key comparison column; r2A's 524px height is the better tradeoff.

general: Allocate width by information role: prose columns need room, but short categorical columns still need enough width to avoid one-word orphans.
A compact table is not automatically better if it fragments repeated key values that readers scan vertically.
Headers may wrap when their data column is narrow, but data values should break at natural phrase boundaries and keep identifiers intact.
Consistent row rhythm helps rows read as units, but content-driven row heights are acceptable when the wrapping is clean.
specific: Billing terms dominates the table (one-line width 490px), so it should receive the largest share of the remaining width.
Minimum seats can be only 87px because only the header wraps; the numeric values still fit.
Contract needs roughly 96–104px: below that, 'Annual only' splits into 'Annual / only', which is visually poor for a short repeated category.
Support below about 130px produces excessive three-line cells; 134px is a reasonable minimum for the common support phrases.

tradeoffs: A designer could prefer r2B or r3B for slightly more Billing or Contract width, or r1A/r3C for a 500px table, accepting fragmented Contract values. There is also a judgment call between keeping Contract clean versus giving Billing enough width to avoid splitting '12-month'.
uncertain: The exact Support threshold where wrapping becomes distracting (130 vs 134 vs 143) and whether the 24px height saving of r1A/r3C is worth the repeated Contract fragmentation. Reasonable designers may also prefer r2C for its wider Support column despite the narrower Billing column.

critique.good: Plan at 96 keeps plan names on one line, and Billing terms at 294 gives the prose a generous measure, so most billing cells stay at 1–2 lines. The Price group hierarchy is clear.
critique.problems: Contract and Support are visibly cramped, so most data rows become 3 lines and the table is tall at 593px despite the wide Billing column. The “List price” header wraps awkwardly, and “Minimum seats” wraps even though its values are only 1–2 digits.
critique.cause: Contract 84 leaves only 63px of text, forcing “Monthly or annual” to 3 lines; Support 100 leaves 79px, also forcing 3 lines. Billing 294 is over-provisioned at 273px of text, while List 58 is below the 67px header one-line width and Minimum seats 87 only just fits “Minimum”.

critique.good: All column headers fit on one line. List price 88 is a clean numeric anchor, Billing 221 keeps prose to 2–3 lines, and there are no mid-word splits.
critique.problems: Minimum seats 130 is mostly empty for 1–2 digit values, while Contract 84 and Support 100 still force 3-line cells. Rows remain 83px and the right side still reads cramped. Business billing also breaks at the “12-” hyphen.
critique.cause: The 43px extra on Minimum seats is unavailable to Contract and Support. Contract text width 63px and Support text width 79px trigger 3-line wraps, while Billing 221 leaves 200px of text, just enough to break “12-month”.

critique.good: Contract 105 and Support 144 make the right-hand constraints much easier to compare; most Contract and Support cells become 2 lines, and Plan 105 is comfortable.
critique.problems: Billing terms is too narrow and drives the table to 640px; several billing sentences become 4 lines, creating uneven tall rows. List price and Minimum seats headers wrap, and Support is wider than Billing, which inverts the prose hierarchy.
critique.cause: Billing 180 gives only 159px of text, below the roughly 200px needed for 3 lines, so Business, Enterprise, and Nonprofit reach 4 lines. List 80 has 59px of text versus the 67px header width; Minimum seats 105 has 84px versus the 109px header width. Support 144 gives 123px, more than most support phrases need.

critique.good: Plan, List price and Minimum seats are stable and readable. Billing terms at 224px gives the prose a clear 2/3-line rhythm and keeps '12-month' intact. Support at 134px lets most labels sit in two lines, and the table stays compact at 500px.
critique.problems: Contract at 90px is visibly too narrow: 'Annual only' and 'Monthly or annual' both wrap into ragged two-line fragments, so the column is hard to scan. Support is still not quite wide enough for 'Dedicated success manager', which takes three lines and makes the Enterprise row taller.
critique.cause: Contract has only 69px of text width, below the ~79px needed for 'Annual only' and the 123px needed for 'Monthly or annual'. Support has 113px, below the 195px one-line width of its longest label.

critique.good: Contract at 102px fixes the ragged Contract column: 'Annual only' now sits on one line. Plan, List price and Minimum seats remain stable, and the header hierarchy is clear.
critique.problems: Support at 125px is cramped: 'Email and chat, 8h response', 'Dedicated success manager' and 'Community forum and email' break into three lines, forcing almost every data row to 83px and making the table 547px tall. Billing terms at 221px also breaks '12-month' at the hyphen in the Business row, which r1A avoided.
critique.cause: Support has only 104px of text width, just below the ~105–115px needed for those two-line groupings. Billing terms has 200px, just below the ~203px that kept '12-month' intact in r1A.

critique.good: Clean left edge: Plan 96 and Minimum seats 87 sit exactly at their longest-word floors (75px, 66px), so headers wrap at spaces and no name breaks. Billing terms at 214 (193 content) comfortably holds 3 lines, and Contract 100 (79) keeps 'Annual only' on one line.
critique.problems: Support 134 (113 content) is just under the width where 'Dedicated success' fits, so the Enterprise row shows 'Dedicated / success / manager' — a 3-line cell competing with the 3-line Billing cell and making the right edge ragged. Contract is also mixed rhythm (1-line 'Annual only' vs 2-line 'Monthly or annual'), and Plan/Minimum seats have zero slack, which is fragile to font rounding.
critique.cause: Support width 134 falls ~1–2px below the ~135 threshold; Contract 100 sits just above the ~99 threshold; Plan 96 and Minimum seats 87 are at hard word floors.

critique.good: Gives the prose column the most room (Billing 216 / 195 content), so Billing breaks fall on sensible phrase boundaries, and Contract 102 (81) safely holds 'Annual only' on one line. Left edge stays compact.
critique.problems: Support 130 (109) is the narrowest of the three, so 'Dedicated success manager' breaks into three lines ('Dedicated / success / manager') — the only non-prose column that exceeds two lines, reading as a ladder. Contract (102) and Support (130) are visually unbalanced yet both wrap.
critique.cause: The 6px shifted from Support relative to r2C went into Billing, which cannot use it: Billing stays 3 lines until roughly 317px width, so the extra width buys nothing while dropping Support below its ~135 threshold.

critique.good: Best of the three: Support 136 (115) lets 'Dedicated success' stay on one line, so only the prose column reaches three lines — the correct hierarchy. Contract 102 keeps 'Annual only' on a single line; Plan and Minimum seats stay at their floors so the table keeps a tight left edge.
critique.problems: Billing terms is squeezed to 210 (189 content), the tightest of the three, producing the awkward hyphen split '12-' / 'month commitment' in Business and a nearly full third line in Nonprofit. Support's 115 content sits ~1px above the wrap threshold, so the clean two-line Support is fragile. Contract is proportionally wide for very short words while the prose column is the narrowest.
critique.cause: 12px was moved from Billing to Support relative to r2A/r2B while Contract stayed at 102; the prose column — which alone sets row height — got the least width of the three.

review.method: two fresh-context blind reviews; letters shuffled; includes browser auto layout and equal widths as neutral references

r1B.why: Balanced widths keep Plan and List price on one line; Billing terms and Support wrap moderately, though Support is tight enough to stack 'Email and chat, 8h response' into three lines.

ref_equal.why: Billing terms is starved: the core descriptions break into five or six short lines, making rows very tall and hard to scan across while other columns keep space they do not need.

r2A.why: Billing terms gets a workable share and rows stay compact, but Contract is too narrow, splitting 'Annual only' and 'Monthly or annual' into awkward two-line chunks.

r2C.why: Best balance: Billing terms dominates as the prose column, Contract and Support are adequate, short Contract values stay intact, and rows read cleanly with consistent wrapping.

ref_auto.why: Billing terms and Support are generously sized, but List price wraps to 'List / price' despite short content, disrupting the Price group's subheader rhythm.

r2B.why: Generally balanced and readable with Contract intact; Support is narrower than in D, forcing 'Community forum and email' into three lines and adding height.

raw.unsure: E is close to D on data-column proportion, but its wrapped 'List price' subheader is a visible hierarchy flaw. I did not penalise the two-line 'Minimum seats' header, which wraps at a natural word boundary in every layout.

r2A.why: Balanced, compact rows: Plan and Minimum seats get generous space, Price sub-columns readable, and only Contract/Support wrap to two lines. Billing terms breaks mid-phrase ("12-/month commitment") and Contract's "Monthly or / annual" is slightly cramped, but overall rhythm is even.

ref_equal.why: Billing terms is starved (~140px) so nearly every cell becomes 5–7 lines; rows are very tall and uneven, the table reads as a column of narrow ribbons rather than scannable rows. Wasted space in Contract/Support while the main descriptive column collapses.

ref_auto.why: Billing terms is comfortable (2–3 lines) and rows stay short and even, but the "List price" header is forced onto two lines while its column stays wide, and the Plan column is tight enough that "Nonprofit" nearly touches the rule — a header hierarchy flaw that costs clarity.

r2C.why: Best proportion: List price just wide enough for its header, Billing terms wide enough for 2–3 line cells, and the right-hand columns sized so Contract/Support wrap evenly at two lines. Row heights are uniform and the eye moves cleanly from plan to price to terms to constraints.

r2B.why: Workable but the right-hand columns are squeezed: Contract wraps "Monthly or / annual" and Support pushes to three lines ("Email and chat, 8h / response"), making rows taller than needed while Billing terms still breaks awkwardly. Nothing broken, just less efficient than D.

r1B.why: Billing terms is narrower than D so descriptive cells run to three lines, and Support is squeezed into three lines as well, inflating row height. The plan and price columns look fine, but the overall vertical stretch makes comparison across rows slower.

raw.unsure: Exact pixel widths can't be measured from the images; D vs A is close, and A might win if a wider Plan/Contract column matters more than compact Billing terms rows. My judgement rests on perceived line counts and row-height uniformity.

provenance.note: AI visual design judgement; not a human reading study
